extracted.intended_audience: People of the State of New York; voters and citizens considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and arguments for evaluating the design and features of the U.S. Senate (qualifications, appointment, representation, size, term, and powers), and related rules for federal elections (locality and timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locality of elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether elections must be held in the counties where the electors resided (a proposed declaration that 'all elections should be had in the counties where the electors resided').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaration of locality would be harmless but afford little additional security; many State constitutions already allow broad latitude (e.g., New York elects Assembly members in counties and Senators in multi-county districts). Centralizing the place of election (e.g., appointing one city as sole place) can exclude remote electors through inconvenience and thus defeat suffrages. The practical effect of an inconvenient place of election is similar whether the distance is twenty miles or twenty thousand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity in the time of elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether times of election for the federal House of Representatives should be uniform across the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity may be of great importance as a security against perpetuation of the same spirit in the body and as a remedy for faction: staggered, different state election times (e.g., between March and November) prevent total dissolution or renovation at once, allowing contagious partisan influence to persist. Uniform election times also facilitate regular rotation in the Senate and convenient annual assembly of the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing election times in the Constitution vs legislative discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a specific election time should be fixed in the Constitution or left to legislative discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fixed constitutional time might be inconvenient upon experiment; entrusting the matter to legislative discretion allows adjustment by experience and preserves convenience (e.g., aligning state and federal election epochs). The supposed danger of gradual change is speculative and does not justify making timing a fundamental constitutional provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: I. The qualification of senators
rubrics_metrics.description: Senatorial qualifications: minimum age and duration of citizenship (senator must be at least 30 years old and have been a citizen nine years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctions from representatives (25 years, 7 years' citizenship) are justified by the senatorial trust needing greater information and stability, and by participation in transactions with foreign nations — thus senators should be more weaned from foreign prepossessions. Nine years is a prudential mediocrity between excluding adopted citizens and admitting them too readily, balancing foreign-influence concerns with merit-based inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: II. Appointment by State legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of constituting the Senate: appointment by State legislatures rather than direct popular election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode is recommended for favoring a select appointment and giving State governments agency in forming the federal government, thereby securing State authority and forming a convenient link between state and federal systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: III. Equality of representation in the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether each State should have equal representation in the Senate (the equality of representation is a compromise between large and small States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality is a constitutional recognition of residuary State sovereignty and an instrument for preserving it; in a compound republic a mixture of proportional and equal representation is appropriate. The equal vote of each State operates as an additional impediment against improper legislation — laws require concurrence first of a majority of the people, then a majority of States — though this check can be both beneficial and occasionally injurious.

rubrics_metrics.name: IV. Number of senators and duration of their appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of how many senators there should be and the length of their terms (the Senate should be less numerous and serve longer terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A smaller and more durably appointed body supplies firmness and permanence: it serves as a salutary check on government by requiring concurrence of two distinct bodies, resists sudden passions and factious leaders, and can devote attention to comprehensive matters of legislation. Longer tenure promotes stability, international respect, continuity of measures, and prevents the harms of frequent legislative turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as a check on government (doubling security)
rubrics_metrics.description: The senate, as a second legislative branch distinct from the first, doubles security to the people by requiring concurrence of two bodies in schemes of usurpation or perfidy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissimilarity in genius between the two bodies makes sinister combinations less probable; therefore the bodies should be distinguished by circumstances consistent with harmony in proper measures and republican principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate to resist sudden and violent passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A senate is needed because numerous single assemblies tend to yield to sudden passions and be seduced by factious leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To correct this infirmity a body should be less numerous and have greater firmness and lengthier tenure to avoid intemperate and pernicious resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate to supply knowledge and legislative expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: A senate addresses the defect that ordinary assemblies, drawn from private pursuits with short terms, lack the time or motive to study laws and national interests thoroughly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many present governmental embarrassments result from legislative blunders; a well-constructed senate provides the continuity and accumulated knowledge to reduce frequent repealing and amending laws and improve wisdom in governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate to provide stability against mutability
rubrics_metrics.description: A senate mitigates the harmful effects of frequent changes in public councils (mutability) which undermine national character, internal order, and long-term planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent turnover forfeits respect of other nations, creates internal incoherence in laws, advantages the moneyed and informed few, damps enterprise, and diminishes attachment to government. A stable senate supports steady policy and national respectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate to safeguard national character and foreign respect
rubrics_metrics.description: A select and stable body preserves a due sense of national character and sensibility to foreign opinion, which is important to merit and obtain the respect and confidence of other nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small, durable assembly will be more affected by praise and blame and thus more likely to consider how measures appear to impartial foreign judgement; this can prevent errors and imprudent measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate to enable responsibility for long-term measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The senate remedies the problem that assemblies elected for short terms cannot be held reasonably responsible for long chains of connected measures whose results occur over years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility must be limited to objects within the power of the responsible party and to operations of that power which constituents can judge; a body with sufficient permanency can be justly answerable for long-term objectives and policy continuities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as defense against popular temporary errors
rubrics_metrics.description: A temperate and respectable senate can check misguided popular measures in critical moments until reason and justice regain the public mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are times when the people, misled by passion or artful misrepresentation, call for measures they will later regret; a stable senate can suspend hasty actions and protect the public from ephemeral errors (examples like Athens are invoked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent for a senate-like institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility of a senate is supported by historical examples: long-lived republics (Sparta, Rome, Carthage) had senatorial institutions that blended stability with liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ancient examples differ from American representative governments, they illustrate that long-lived republics tended to have some stable council; the American difference (principle of representation and exclusion of the people in collective capacity) strengthens the case for a senate adapted to our situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterargument: improbability of senatorial tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection that a senate appointed indirectly and for six years will become tyrannical is addressed by showing the practical difficulties of effecting such a revolution (the Senate would first have to corrupt itself, then state legislatures, then the House, and finally the people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience (e.g., Maryland's indirectly elected senate with similar term) shows no symptoms of the feared danger; the British hereditary upper house is a far more formidable example of aristocracy and thus does not confirm the particular fear about the proposed federal Senate.
